title: The key she did not return
paragraphs: On the morning the flat was to be emptied, my aunt arrived carrying a cake. She had always brought cake to occasions that did not admit of celebration. When my father lost his job, there had been a walnut cake. When my grandmother moved into a room with a number on its door, there had been lemon. Now there was a plain sponge in a tin, still warm enough to cloud the lid. My mother put it on the kitchen table and said we had no plates. This was not true. There were six plates in the cupboard, wrapped for the removal company, and all three of us knew it.

We had been sorting the flat for a week. The decisions that ought to have been difficult had passed quickly: the broken sofa, the curtains faded differently on either side, the radio that could receive only one station. What held us up were small things without an obvious destination. A jar of screws. A train timetable ten years out of date. A photograph of a woman none of us could identify, standing in front of a house none of us remembered. My mother wanted to throw the photograph away. My aunt said somebody might know her. Somebody, I thought, was a very accommodating person, always available in the future to justify keeping things now.

The keys were in a dish beside the door. My father had labelled them with small paper tags, although his handwriting had become harder to read each year. Front door. Cellar. Window. One tag said simply Other. The window key no longer fitted any window in the flat; the frames had been replaced long before. We agreed it could go. The cellar key was needed by the new owner. The key marked Other was smaller than the rest and had a bright groove along its edge. My aunt picked it up and put it in her coat pocket while my mother was looking for the kettle. I pretended not to see.

At lunch, if the handful of cake we ate standing up deserved that name, my mother asked whether there were any more keys. My aunt said no. She said it without hesitation, looking directly at my mother, as if she had prepared the answer before coming. I might have corrected her. Instead I washed the tin, which gave me something to do with my hands. It is easy, afterwards, to give silence a generous explanation. I have sometimes told myself I was protecting my aunt. At the time, I suspect, I was avoiding a conversation whose ending I could not control. Those are not quite the same thing.

The removal men came at two. They were careful with the furniture and careless with the names, calling my mother by my grandmother’s name because it was on the contract. My mother corrected them once, then let it stand. My aunt followed each box to the door as though an extra pair of eyes could make the journey safe. Only when the table was carried out did she stop. There was a pale rectangle on the floor where the sunlight had never reached. For a moment the room seemed more occupied by that absence than by any of us. We stood around it, giving a piece of unmarked floor the attention we had refused to give the cake.

Outside, my mother handed over the keys and checked the list again. The new owner asked about the small one marked Other. There was an entry for it in the paperwork. My mother said it must have been thrown away with the old window key. My aunt nodded. I cannot remember whether I nodded too. That failure of memory has become convenient, and I distrust it. I remember the shape of the tin, the printer’s blue ink on the removal contract and a loose button on my aunt’s sleeve. It would be strange if I had genuinely forgotten only the small movement by which I agreed to the story.

Months later, I visited my aunt. The key lay on her kitchen shelf beside a cup that nobody used. She did not hide it. When I asked what it opened, she said she had no idea. I waited for a story about my father, a childhood hiding place or a box of letters. None came. She said she liked having something that still expected an answer. I would have thought a remembered object needed a remembered purpose. She had kept, instead, the possibility that there had been a purpose she did not know. The key was no more a record than a wish is, but I found I no longer wanted to make that objection aloud.

I have not told my mother. This omission looks worse on paper than it feels during an ordinary afternoon, which may be why people avoid writing things down. I could claim that the key has no practical value. Yet the new owner had asked for it, and the question of value was not mine alone to settle. Nor was my aunt’s attachment a permission I could issue on her behalf. If I tell the story carefully enough, I can make every person appear reasonable. That is another way of not deciding. The key remains on the shelf. Each time I visit, I notice whether it has moved, and my aunt notices me noticing.

Last Sunday she offered me the unused cup. I said I had enough cups at home. She smiled and made tea in it anyway. We drank at the table, without discussing the key or the flat, and there was no cake. When I left, she asked whether I had everything. I felt in my pocket for my own keys and said yes. She waited a moment before closing the door.
translation: 清空公寓那天，姑母带蛋糕来。她总在不适庆祝的场合带蛋糕：父亲失业时核桃，祖母住进有号码房间时柠檬。今天温海绵蛋糕使盒盖起雾。母亲说没盘，其实柜有六只已包装，我们都知道。
整理一周，本应难的沙发窗帘收音机很快定，反倒小物无归处拖延：螺丝、过时时刻表、无人识别的人房旧照。母亲要丢，姑母说或有人认得。我想“有人”真方便，总在未来替现在留物作理由。
钥匙在门边碟里，父亲纸签字越发难读：前门、地下室、窗、其他。换窗多年旧窗钥匙可丢，地下室给新主。其他小且亮槽。姑母趁母亲找壶收进口袋，我装没看。
站着吃点蛋糕算午饭时，母亲问还有钥匙否。姑母直视答没有，似预备好了。我可纠正却去洗盒让手有事。事后易给沉默高尚理由，我有时说护姑母，当时恐怕是避不可控谈话，两者不同。
搬运工两点来，搬物细却叫错名，合同祖母名而非母亲；她纠一次后算了。姑母目送每箱，桌抬走才停，地板晒不到的浅长方仿佛比我们更占房。围着未标地板，却曾不肯关注蛋糕。
外面交钥匙时，新主问文件列的其他。母亲说应与旧窗钥匙丢了，姑母点头。我不记是否也点头；方便的失忆令我怀疑。蛋盒、合同蓝墨、姑母松扣都记，只忘自己同意故事的小动作便奇怪。
月后姑母厨房架上钥匙未藏。问开什么，她不知，我等父亲童年藏处或信盒故事却无。她说喜欢还有东西等待答案。我原以为记物须记用途，她留的是可能曾有未知用途。钥匙如愿望非记录，我却不想说反驳。
尚未告诉母亲。纸上省略比普通下午感觉更糟，或是人不写原因。可称无实用值，但新主问过、价值非我定；姑母依恋也非我可发许可。我若细讲可让人人合理，也是逃决定。每次察钥匙动否，她察我察。
上周日她赠无人用杯，我说够了。她笑仍用它泡茶。桌边喝，不谈钥匙公寓，也没蛋糕。走时问带齐否，我摸自己钥匙答是，她等片刻才关门。

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator distrust the missing memory of nodding?
options: It conveniently removes their own visible agreement while other details remain vivid.
They have forgotten every detail of the move.
The aunt later proved no one nodded.
questions.explanation: 第六段承认选择性失忆便利，非证据证明没有点头。

questions.prompt: What does the remark about “somebody” initially reveal?
options: Certainty that the photographed woman will be identified.
A plan to ask the new owner immediately.
The narrator’s scepticism toward deferring decisions through an imagined future person.
questions.explanation: 第二段用讽刺指出“有人”给拖延留物作借口。

questions.prompt: What does the aunt say the key opens?
options: The cellar of the old flat.
She says she does not know.
A box of her brother’s letters.
questions.explanation: 第七段没有提供期待的怀旧解释。

questions.prompt: What does “no more a record than a wish is” imply in context?
options: The key cannot serve as reliable evidence of its unknown history.
Both keys and wishes are complete historical records.
The key has more financial value than the cup.
questions.explanation: 修辞比较否定记录功能，而非否定感情价值。

questions.prompt: Which interpretation best fits the ending?
options: The narrator confesses everything and returns the key.
The aunt confirms the key was legally hers.
The ordinary exchange leaves the narrator’s complicity unresolved.
questions.explanation: 末段仍日常含糊，带齐的问话呼应未解决的钥匙责任。

title: The forecast that knew too much
paragraphs: The first forecast arrived as a single figure with two decimal places. Our town, it said, would need 18.37 per cent more water in ten years. At the public meeting, that precision seemed to settle the matter before questions began. A councillor repeated the figure while pointing to a map of proposed pipes. Residents discussed the cost, the route and which streets would be closed during construction. Few asked how the forecast had been made. The number did not force anyone to accept the plan, but it gave the plan an air of necessity. Decisions still requiring judgement were presented beside a result that looked as though judgement had already ended.

Later, a researcher explained that the model used assumptions about population, household size and seasonal demand. Each assumption was defensible, but none was certain. Small changes in them produced a range of plausible outcomes. The exact figure was the output of one selected scenario, not a measurement of water that the future had somehow already delivered. The software could calculate precisely from the inputs without making those inputs precise. This distinction is elementary when stated plainly, yet it becomes easy to forget when a polished chart and an authoritative speaker put an uncertain estimate into the visual form of a completed fact.

It would be unfair to accuse the researcher of pretending to know the future. She had included a technical note describing the assumptions. The note was several pages from the main chart, however, and its language presumed familiarity with modelling. A qualification that exists somewhere in a document is not necessarily a qualification that shapes its public meaning. The most memorable figure travels faster than the explanation that limits it. By the time the forecast appeared in a local headline, the conditional nature of the scenario had vanished. Nobody needed to invent a false number for the claim to become misleading; removing the conditions was enough.

There is an equally tempting mistake in the other direction. Once uncertainty is exposed, opponents may argue that no investment should proceed. But a range of futures is no more a reason for inaction than an exact-looking figure is a command to build. Planning requires choices before all conditions are known. The relevant question is not whether the model is certain, but which decisions remain sensible across several plausible outcomes and which depend heavily on one assumption. A smaller first stage might be useful in many scenarios, whereas a particular expansion could require evidence that demand is rising. Uncertainty should organise a decision rather than serve as a universal veto.

For the next meeting, the researcher presented three scenarios and stated what would change the recommendation. She also showed which data the town could collect over the following two years. The audience now had something more demanding than a number to remember: a relationship between evidence and action. If household demand rose beyond a stated range, a further review would be triggered. If population growth slowed, the larger proposal would be reconsidered. These were not promises that events would behave conveniently. They were commitments about how the council would respond when events did not match the preferred story. A forecast became a tool for learning rather than an announcement of fate.

Some residents preferred the earlier certainty. They wanted to know whether their street would be dug up, not attend a lesson in conditional reasoning. Their frustration was understandable. Public participation should not require everyone to become a specialist. It does require officials to distinguish what is decided from what is being estimated. The route for the initial work could be stated clearly, even if later stages remained contingent. An honest answer can contain both a firm commitment and an explicit uncertainty. Treating everything as provisional makes accountability slippery; treating everything as settled makes revision look like failure. The task is to draw the boundary in a place that readers can actually find.

The two decimal places eventually disappeared from the headline. That was a modest improvement, not proof that communication had become perfect. A round number can mislead just as effectively if its conditions remain hidden. Nor does presenting three scenarios guarantee that the least powerful residents will be heard. Someone must still decide whose costs enter the model and which disruptions are treated as acceptable. The technical question of what may happen is inseparable from the political question of who is asked to bear the consequences. Better numerical language cannot settle that question, but it can stop a calculation from appearing to have settled it on everyone’s behalf.

I kept the original leaflet. When I look at it now, the most striking feature is not the figure but the absence of verbs showing a choice. The town “will require” water; the pipes “will provide” it. Nobody in those sentences decides, tests or revises. A useful forecast needs those human actions around it. It should tell us not only what a model produces, but what we are prepared to do with the result, what might make us change course and who remains answerable when we do.
translation: 镇用水十年预测18.37%增，两位小数似先定问题。议员拿数字指管图，居民谈钱路封街，少问预测来历。数字不强迫，却给计划必然感，尚需判断的决定旁摆似已结束判断的结果。
研究者说明模型用人口、户大小、季需求假设，各可辩但不确定，稍变得合理范围。精数字是选情景输出非未来已送水的测量。软件精算不使输入精确，简单区别却易在漂亮图和权威言语下遗忘。
不应指她伪装预知，她附技术假设说明却离图几页且需建模知识。文件某处有限制不等于限制塑公共意义，数字比限制传得快，新闻已丢情景条件。不用造假数，删条件就可误导。
另一极端：显露未知便反对投资。但多未来非不行动理由，正如精数非必建命令。须先未知中选；问哪些多情景合理、哪些押单假设。小阶段可多案用，扩建须需求证据。未知应组织决定非万能否决。
下会列三情景及改推荐条件，说明两年可采数据。居民需记证据-行动关系：户需求超范围再评、人口慢重新考虑大案。非保证事情顺，而承诺不符时如何回应，预测成学习工具非命运宣告。
有人要旧确定性，只想知自街是否挖，非条件推理课， 不耐烦合理。参与非人人专家，而官须分已定与估计。初段路线可定、后段有条件。诚实答同时含诺和未知；全暂定责任滑，全定修改像失败，须边界可找。
新闻终删两小数，仅小改善，整数隐藏条件也误导，三情景非保证弱者被听。仍须定谁成本入模、何种打扰可接受。会发生什么和谁承受不可分，更好数字语言不能定政治，却可防计算代大家定。
我留旧单，如今最醒目非数字而缺选择动词：镇“将需”、管“将供”，无人决定、测试、修改。好预测需周围人的动作，告诉结果怎用、何使改向、谁仍负责。

grammar.surface: no more a reason for inaction than

questions.prompt: What role should uncertainty play in planning?
options: Prevent any investment until the future is measured directly.
Justify the preferred plan regardless of new evidence.
Shape conditional decisions and revision rules without either pretending certainty or prohibiting all action.
questions.explanation: 全文反对假确定与万能否决，提证据触发的调整。

questions.prompt: Why was the original number misleading despite being a genuine model output?
options: Every estimate with decimals is fraudulent.
Its scenario conditions were not visible in the public claim.
The model could not perform arithmetic.
questions.explanation: 第二三段区分精算与假设确定，传播删条件。

questions.prompt: What would happen if population growth slowed in the revised plan?
options: The larger proposal would be reconsidered.
All residents would pay the same fee.
The first stage would automatically double.
questions.explanation: 第五段明述人口慢会重新考虑大方案。

questions.prompt: What does “not necessarily a qualification that shapes its public meaning” deny?
options: The existence of the technical note.
The possibility of honest qualifications at all.
The inevitability that a written caveat influences readers’ understanding.
questions.explanation: not necessarily否定必然关系，未否定说明存在。

questions.prompt: Why close by discussing missing choice verbs?
options: To suggest pipes themselves should make political decisions.
To expose how apparently inevitable wording obscures human responsibility.
To recommend writing reports without any future tense.
questions.explanation: 末段把预测置回决定测试修订与责任的人的活动。

title: The letter that refused its title
paragraphs: The letter entered the archive under the title “A daughter’s farewell.” Written on thin paper, it described a train journey, a borrowed coat and the writer’s hope that her mother would not worry. The catalogue placed it among documents of permanent migration. A reader encountering the title before the page could readily imagine a final departure, with the journey standing for a decisive separation from home. Yet the letter itself contained a practical question: should the writer bring the sewing machine back when she returned in autumn? That question did not disprove a later migration. It did complicate the apparent finality of the farewell we had been invited to read.

The archivist who had created the entry was no longer available to explain it. A note on the folder suggested that the donor had described the writer as an aunt who eventually settled abroad. It was therefore plausible that the title had been influenced by knowledge of the ending. We do this frequently when reading older material: we allow what happened afterwards to reorganise what a person could have known at the time. An uncertain journey becomes the beginning of a settled biography. A temporary intention becomes a symbolic farewell. The resulting story may be coherent, but coherence is not proof that its emphasis belongs to the original writer.

A colleague argued that the existing title should remain because it made the document easier to find. Visitors looking for accounts of migration were more likely to search for farewell than for sewing machine. This was not a trivial concern. Material that cannot be located is scarcely available to public use, however carefully it has been preserved. But usefulness in a search system should not silently determine the interpretation offered to a reader. We could keep migration as a subject term while changing the displayed title to a description of the journey. The choice was not between perfect neutrality and total inaccessibility. It was between making a catalogue judgement visible and allowing it to masquerade as the letter’s own declaration. We recommended that the catalogue keep both the subject term and the account of its revision.

The distinction matters especially when the writer has left few records. A famous author may be represented by enough documents for a misleading label to be challenged. An ordinary person can be reduced to one page and one sentence about it. If that sentence turns her into a representative example, the details that resist the category may look incidental. The borrowed coat becomes evidence of hardship; concern for her mother becomes evidence of separation; the sewing machine becomes an irrelevant household object. In the letter, those details may have been the point. They connect the journey to continuing obligations rather than announce a clean break from them.

We drafted a revised entry stating what was known and how it was known. The donor’s account indicated that the writer later lived abroad. The letter suggested an intention to return in autumn. Neither statement was made to cancel the other. A plan can change, and an intention recorded on one date cannot stand for an entire life. We also noted that the original catalogue title had interpreted the journey as a farewell. Retaining that history of description allowed future readers to examine our own intervention. An archive is not improved by pretending that it has suddenly escaped interpretation; it is improved when interpretations can be identified, compared and revised. We retained the old entry lest its influence be forgotten.

There was a temptation to give the letter a more attractive new story: perhaps it demonstrated that migration is always a negotiation between leaving and belonging. That may be a fruitful argument for an essay, but attaching it to the catalogue would merely replace one large claim with another. Not every departure carries the same meaning, and not all letters are attempts to explain identity. This one also asked whether a parcel had arrived and reminded the mother to pay a neighbour. The writer may have been thinking about larger questions, but the page did not authorise us to supply them. Close reading sometimes requires declining an interpretation that sounds more elegant than the evidence permits.

For a small exhibition, we displayed the letter beside its two descriptions. Visitors could compare the old title with the revised account and identify details each one emphasised. Some preferred the original because it offered a stronger emotional shape. Others liked the unanswered question of the return. We did not ask them to vote for the correct feeling. We asked which claims could be supported by the page and which depended on information outside it. This shifted the exercise from judging whether a label was moving to examining what kind of authority it claimed. A compelling story might still be possible, but its source and its limits would remain part of the story.

The revised entry did not make the archive complete. The coat’s owner remained unknown, the autumn journey uncertain and the sewing machine untraced. These gaps were not errors we could correct by choosing warmer language. Nor did they make the document useless. They defined the questions the letter could reasonably prompt. The most responsible description was therefore neither a refusal to say anything nor a confident account of a life we could not recover. It gave readers enough context to approach the page while leaving its resistance intact. The letter was allowed to concern a woman travelling somewhere, carrying obligations with her, rather than merely a daughter performing the farewell that our title had prepared.
translation: 信档标题“女儿的告别”，写火车、借外套、希望母亲别担心，被归永久迁移。先见标题易以为最后离乡，信却问秋返是否带缝纫机。非否定后来迁移，但挑战标题引导的最终性。
建条者不在，夹注说捐者称姑母最终海外定居，因此标题可能受结局影响。读旧材料常让后来事重组当时所知，把未知旅变传记开端、暂意变象征告别。顺畅非原作者重点证据。
同事说“告别”易被迁移研究者检索，非小顾虑，保存却找不到也难公共用。但检索用途不应暗定解读。可留迁移主题词、改显示旅程标题，非中立与不可达二选，而显露目录判断还是伪装信自述。 我们建议目录同时保留主题词和修订说明。
记录少者尤要紧，名家多文可反标签，普通人或仅一页一说明。代表例标签使抗类别细节变偶然：借外套变困苦、担母变分离、缝纫机变琐事；信中这些可能正重点，旅与持续责任相连非斩断。
修订区分已知与来源：捐述后来海外，信示秋返意图，互不取消，计划会变、一次意图非全生命。留旧标题作为目录解读史，让后人检视我们的介入。档案非突然脱解释才好，而解释可辨比较修改。 我们保留旧条目，以免其影响被遗忘。
又想给更美故事：迁移总是离与归协商，作文或有益，贴目录只是换大断言。非每离同义、每信析身份；本信还问包裹、提醒付邻人。也许想大问题却页无授权我们补，细读有时须拒比证据优雅的解释。
展时并列两描述，观众比细节重点，有人爱旧情绪形、有人爱未答归问。不投正确感情，而问何断言有页据、何靠页外。由标签感人否移到它声称何权威；故事仍可动人，但来源界限属其中。
修条非全档：外套主人、秋返、缝机仍未知，非改温词可补，也非令信无用，而界定可问。负责任描述非拒说也非自信重建无法找回生命，给语境留抗性。让信讲带责任旅人，不仅演标题预备的女儿告别。

grammar.surface: however carefully it has been preserved

questions.prompt: What does the revised cataloguing approach aim to do?
options: Replace every uncertain detail with a more uplifting story.
Expose the sources and limits of interpretation without making the letter unfindable.
Remove all subject terms related to migration.
questions.explanation: 第三五段兼顾发现性与可检查解释。

questions.prompt: Which detail resists reading the letter as an unequivocal final departure?
options: The question about bringing a sewing machine back in autumn.
The fact that the paper is thin.
The later donor’s reference to an aunt abroad.
questions.explanation: 第一段秋返提问限制最终告别解读。

questions.prompt: Why can an ordinary writer be especially vulnerable to a catalogue label?
options: Ordinary writers never intended to return home.
Famous authors’ catalogues are always neutral.
Few surviving records may leave little evidence through which to challenge it.
questions.explanation: 第四段相比多文名家，单一记录更易被一句代表。

questions.prompt: What does “not all letters are attempts to explain identity” permit?
options: Every letter concerns identity but hides it.
Some letters may concern identity, while the category is not universal.
No letter can concern identity.
questions.explanation: 部分否定限制全称，不全面否定。

questions.prompt: Why retain the history of the original description?
options: To make the archive’s own interpretive changes available for scrutiny.
To prove the earlier archivist acted maliciously.
To tell visitors the old title remains the only correct one.
questions.explanation: 第五段保解释变动供后人辨比较修改。

title: The promise of an empty hour
paragraphs: A friend gave me an hourglass with a note suggesting that I reserve one hour each evening for concentrated work. The object was handsome: dark wood, clear glass, sand that seemed almost reluctant to fall. I placed it beside my books and imagined that its physical presence would protect the hour from interruption. Unlike a timer on my telephone, it offered no invitation to inspect a message while checking the time. For several evenings, the arrangement worked. I read, made notes and enjoyed the quiet drama of an object doing nothing but measuring the limit I had chosen. Then an ordinary week arrived and exposed how much the experiment had borrowed from unusually favourable circumstances.

On Monday, a neighbour needed help carrying a parcel upstairs. On Tuesday, a family call lasted longer than expected. On Wednesday, I was simply tired. None of these events resembled the distractions that advice about concentration usually names. There was no endless stream of entertainment, no irresistible advertisement, no failure to turn off a notification. The demands came from relationships I valued and from a body that did not regard a handsome hourglass as an instruction. I could have classified each event as an interruption and defended the hour more firmly. But that description would already have made a judgement about which parts of my life were supposed to yield to which others.

The familiar language of productivity encourages this judgement to disappear into a technique. Schedule the hour, remove the device, block the site. These can be useful actions, but they do not decide what the hour is for or what claim it has on other people. Concentration is not an isolated virtue. Someone who appears wonderfully focused may have another person answering the door, arranging dinner or responding to family needs. If those conditions are omitted, a method can look like a personal quality available to anyone willing to try. Its unequal support becomes the invisible background against which others are told to measure their failure.

This does not imply that an uninterrupted hour is undeserved or that every request must be accepted. A person who always makes space for others can lose the chance to pursue work that matters deeply. The point is that boundaries need reasons and sometimes negotiation, not merely stronger enforcement. I began telling people when I planned to read and asking whether anything required my attention beforehand. I also distinguished urgency from convenience. A request to move a heavy parcel could wait until the sand had fallen; a distressed relative might not. No device could make that distinction for me without also being given a set of values about how I should live.

The hour became shorter on some evenings and less negotiable on others. Curiously, that made it easier to keep. It was no longer an ideal interval against which every ordinary demand counted as damage. It was an arrangement whose purpose I could explain. I read to follow an argument carefully, not to demonstrate that I could remain still for sixty minutes. When fatigue made that purpose impossible, I stopped rather than leaving the hourglass running beside an unread page. A visible measure can help maintain a practice, but it can also tempt us to preserve the measure after the practice has disappeared. The sand does not know the difference between attention and endurance.

I was also surprised by what happened to the telephone. I had assumed its absence would solve the main problem. Sometimes it did. At other times, I found a reason to leave the desk, wash a cup or reorganise a shelf. The device had been an available route away from difficulty, not necessarily its source. That observation did not make the design of digital services irrelevant. Systems can certainly exploit a moment of hesitation. It did suggest that removing one route would not teach me how to remain with a difficult paragraph. For that, I needed a smaller task, a question to answer and permission to reread without treating slow progress as evidence of incompetence.
It is important for us to distinguish a useful boundary from a claim to other people’s time. That distinction is not made once and settled forever; it depends on responsibilities that can change.

Advice tends to travel most easily when it becomes an object or a rule. An hourglass can be photographed; a negotiated boundary cannot. “One hour every evening” is memorable; “protect enough time for the purpose, while reviewing who makes that protection possible” is not. The loss of complexity is understandable, but it is not innocent when the simple version becomes a moral test. The person who cannot reproduce the visible ritual may assume that they lack discipline, rather than noticing that the arrangement presumes a quieter home, a different job or another person’s labour. A method should invite adaptation to those conditions, not make them disappear behind an attractive picture.

The hourglass still stands beside my books. Occasionally I turn it over for a full hour; sometimes I read without touching it. It is useful precisely because I no longer ask it to certify that the evening was well spent. I have kept the friend’s note too. Its generosity lay in offering me time, not in prescribing the exact shape of that time. To treat the gift as a contract would have been to miss its point. What I wanted was not an empty hour from which life had been excluded. It was a way to give one chosen activity sufficient room within a life that remained populated by other people.
translation: 朋友送沙漏建议每晚一小时专心，木玻沙漂亮。我想物理存在护时，非手机计时顺便看消息。几晚奏效，读记享它只量选择边界。普通一周来了，显实验借了异常顺利条件多少。
周一帮邻搬包，周二家电久，周三只是累，非通常分心娱乐广告通知，而珍重关系和不听沙漏身体。可归中断强护，但已先判何部分生活应让另部分。
效率语言让判断藏技术：排时、移设备、封站有用却不定用途或对别人权利。专注非孤德，专注者或有人接门、做饭、应家事。省条件后方法像人人努力可得品质，不平等支援成衡失败隐背景。
非说无中断不配或请求都接，永给别人可失重要工作。边界需理由协商非只强执行。我先告读时、问此前需否，再分急与便：重包可等、焦虑亲属可能不可。设备没生活价值设置便不能代分。
有晚时短、有晚不可协商，反易维持。非理想区间遇日常即损，而可解释安排。读为跟论证非证静坐六十分。累不能便停不让漏旁空读。可见量帮实践，也诱保量当实践失；沙不辨注意与耐受。
也惊手机：缺席有时帮，有时改洗杯理架。设备是逃难路线、未必源，非否认数字设计可利用犹豫。但去一路非教留难段，须小任务、可答问、准重读，不把慢当无能。
对我们而言，区分有用的边界与对他人时间的要求很重要。这不是一次定案的区分，而取决于可能变化的责任。
建议成物或规则易传：沙漏可拍，协商边界不行；每晚一时易记，护目的且审谁支持难记。简化可理解，变道德考却不无辜；复制不了仪式者自责无纪律，未见静家不同工作或他人劳动前提。方法应邀按条件适应非漂亮图掩。
沙漏仍旁，有时翻满时、有时不碰读。因不再让它认证晚间好，才有用。朋友纸条也留，慷慨在赠时间非定精形，把礼当合同会错。我非想排生活空一时，而让选择活动在有他人生活中获足够空间。

questions.prompt: What revision of concentration advice does the writer advocate?
options: Adapt protected time to its purpose and relational conditions rather than treating a ritual as proof of virtue.
Accept every request and abandon private work.
Replace every digital timer with an hourglass.
questions.explanation: 全文仍护专注，却目的及他人条件可见，不仪式道德化。

questions.prompt: What is meant by saying the sand cannot distinguish attention from endurance?
options: Hourglasses never measure time correctly.
Fatigue is always caused by reading fiction.
Completing a duration does not prove meaningful engagement.
questions.explanation: 第五段分真正跟论证与只坚持坐时间。

questions.prompt: What did removing the telephone reveal?
options: Digital service design ceased to matter.
The writer sometimes found other ways to avoid a difficult task.
All problems disappeared permanently.
questions.explanation: 第六段改洗杯理架，且仍承认数字设计影响。

questions.prompt: What does “not necessarily its source” imply about the device?
options: It may provide an escape route without being the cause in every case.
It is proved never to cause distraction.
It is always the sole cause of avoidance.
questions.explanation: not necessarily限定必然因果，非证无影响。

questions.prompt: Why contrast a photographable hourglass with an invisible negotiated boundary?
options: To argue that no object can ever be useful.
To recommend photographing every conversation.
To show how shareable simplicity can hide the conditions sustaining a practice.
questions.explanation: 第七段解释可传播规则抹支撑条件、可能成不公测试。

notes: 练习重点：根据正文证据回答，区分事实、推断和作者评价。
